literal: By nature Rou was rather gentle yet quite stubborn and self-willed—that was what people heard; Shou often resented and feared him.
idiomatic: By nature Rou was pliant in disposition yet stubborn and set in his ways—that was the reputation he bore; Wei Shou often resented and feared him.

literal: He also took part in deliberating statutes and ordinances.
idiomatic: He also took part in deliberating statutes and ordinances.

literal: At the time deliberators held that in establishing the five ranks of enfeoffment and fiefs, when the inheritor had no direct son one established the direct grandson; when there was no direct grandson, the direct younger brother of the son; when there was no direct younger brother of the son, the direct younger brother of the grandson.
idiomatic: At the time deliberators held that in establishing the five ranks of enfeoffment and fiefs, if the heir had no eldest son one named the eldest grandson; if no eldest grandson, the eldest son's younger brother; if none of those, the grandson's younger brother.

literal: Rou held that when there was no direct grandson one ought to establish the direct great-grandson, and one should not establish the direct younger brother of the son.
idiomatic: Rou held that without an eldest grandson one ought to name the eldest great-grandson, and ought not name the eldest son's younger brother.

literal: The deliberation states:
idiomatic: The deliberation reads:

literal: Rou cites the Rites: establishing the heir by seniority is why the eldest son is called the direct son.
idiomatic: Rou cites the Rites: the heir is established by seniority, which is why the eldest son is called the direct heir.

literal: When the direct son dies, take the direct son's son as direct grandson; when he dies, great-grandson and great-great-grandson follow the same rule.
idiomatic: When the direct heir dies, his son becomes the direct grandson; when that grandson dies, great-grandson and great-great-grandson follow in the same way.

literal: Thus the name direct son exists fundamentally to transmit the main line.
idiomatic: The title direct heir exists, then, to carry the main ancestral line.

literal: Hence the Mourning Dress says: A son by a concubine does not wear mourning three years for the eldest son—he does not continue grandfather and father.
idiomatic: Hence the Mourning Dress says, "A son by a concubine does not mourn the eldest son for three years—he does not continue grandfather and father."

literal: Record of Rites, the mourning for Gongyi Zhongzi: Zhan Gong said, What is this? I have never heard of it before.
idiomatic: In the Record of Rites, on the mourning for Gongyi Zhongzi: Zhan Gong said, "What is this? I have never heard of it before."

literal: Why did Zhongzi set aside his grandson and establish his son?
idiomatic: "Why did Zhongzi set aside his grandson and name his son instead?"

literal: Zifu Bozi said: Zhongzi was also following the ancient way. In former times King Wen set aside Bo Yi Kao and established King Wu Fa; Weizi set aside his grandson Dun and established his younger brother Yan—Zhongzi too was following the ancient way.
idiomatic: Zifu Bozi said, "Zhongzi was also following the ancient way. Long ago King Wen set aside Bo Yi Kao and established King Wu Fa; Weizi set aside his grandson Dun and established his younger brother Yan—Zhongzi too was following the ancient way."

literal: Zheng's commentary says: Bozi was speaking euphemistically for a kinsman; establishing the son was not correct.
idiomatic: Zheng's commentary says, "Bozi was speaking euphemistically for a kinsman; naming the son was not correct."

literal: King Wen's establishing King Wu was an expedient.
idiomatic: King Wen's establishing King Wu was an expedient.

literal: When Weizi's direct son died he established his younger brother Yan—Yin rites.
idiomatic: When Weizi's direct heir died he established his younger brother Yan—that was Yin rites.

literal: Ziyou asked Confucius; Confucius said: No—establish the grandson.
idiomatic: "Ziyou asked Confucius; Confucius said, 'No—establish the grandson.'"

literal: The commentary says: according to the Rites of Zhou.
idiomatic: The commentary says, "According to the Rites of Zhou."

literal: Thus in Shang, when the direct son died, they established the mother's younger brother of the direct son; in Zhou, when the direct son died, they established the direct son's son as direct grandson.
idiomatic: Thus in Shang, when the direct heir died, they named his mother's younger brother; in Zhou, when the direct heir died, they named his son as direct grandson.

literal: Thus the meaning of the Gongyang Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals: when the direct son has a grandson and dies, in the quality-oriented school kinship comes first and the younger brother is established; in the culture-oriented school honor comes first and the grandson is established.
idiomatic: Thus the Gongyang reading of the Spring and Autumn Annals: when the direct heir has a grandson and dies, the quality-oriented school, prizing kinship, establishes the younger brother first; the culture-oriented school, prizing rank, establishes the grandson first.

literal: The Mourning Dress says: One who becomes heir to the father wears no mourning for an expelled mother.
idiomatic: The Mourning Dress says, "One who becomes heir to the father wears no mourning for an expelled mother."

literal: The Lesser Record says: When the grandfather dies, one who thereafter becomes heir to the grandmother wears mourning three years.
idiomatic: The Lesser Record says, "When the grandfather dies, one who thereafter becomes heir to the grandmother wears mourning three years."

literal: The reason one who becomes heir to the father wears no mourning for an expelled mother is that the mourner does not sacrifice to her.
idiomatic: He who becomes heir to the father wears no mourning for an expelled mother because the heir does not sacrifice to her.

literal: The reason one wears three years for the grandmother is that the great lineage transmits the main line.
idiomatic: He wears three years for the grandmother because the great lineage carries the main ancestral weight.

literal: Now the deliberation would, when the direct grandson dies, establish the mother's younger brother of the direct son; the mother's younger brother of the direct son would then become heir to the father.
idiomatic: Now the deliberation would, when the direct grandson dies, name the direct son's mother's younger brother—who would then become heir to the father.

literal: The mother's younger brother of the direct son was originally not one who could inherit the direct line; only because there was no direct heir could he become heir to the father.
idiomatic: That younger brother was never meant to inherit the direct line; only the absence of a direct heir would let him become heir to the father.

literal: Then by principle the younger brother of the direct grandson should also be able to become heir to the father.
idiomatic: By the same logic the direct grandson's younger brother ought to be able to become heir to the father.

literal: Then one would wear the severest mourning for having become heir to the grandfather after the father's death; having obtained the right to mourn the grandfather with the severest grade, yet not being able to transmit the main line—I have never heard of such a thing.
idiomatic: Then one would wear the severest mourning for becoming grandfather's heir only after the father's death—yet having earned that severest grade for the grandfather, one could not carry the main line. I have never heard of such a thing.

literal: If one applied the Shang school's meaning of prizing kinship, one originally should not, when the direct son died, establish the direct grandson.
idiomatic: If one followed the Shang school's kinship-first rule, one should not, when the direct heir died, establish the direct grandson at all.

literal: If one followed the Zhou school's culture of honoring rank, how could one set aside the grandson and establish the younger brother?
idiomatic: If one followed the Zhou school's honor-first rule, how could one set aside the grandson and name the younger brother?

literal: Whether culture or quality, I am perplexed in using them.
idiomatic: Culture or quality—whichever one follows, I remain perplexed.

literal: The Lesser Record also says: When the direct daughter-in-law does not become heir to father-in-law and mother-in-law, then the father's sisters wear mourning in the lesser grade.
idiomatic: The Lesser Record also says, "When the direct daughter-in-law does not become heir to her parents-in-law, the husband's sisters wear the lesser grade of mourning."

literal: The commentary says: meaning when the husband has crippling illness or other cause, or dies without a son who can receive the main line.
idiomatic: The commentary says this means when the husband has crippling illness or some other cause, or dies without a son who can receive the main line.

literal: Lesser grade is the dress of a concubine's wife.
idiomatic: The lesser grade is the dress of a concubine's wife.

literal: Whenever parents toward sons, or parents-in-law toward daughters-in-law, are about not to transmit the main line to the direct heir, or the one about to receive the transmitted main line is not the direct heir, the mourning worn is all like that for ordinary sons and concubines' wives.
idiomatic: Whenever parents toward sons, or parents-in-law toward daughters-in-law, will not transmit the main line to the direct heir—or will transmit it to someone who is not the direct heir—the mourning worn is always that for ordinary sons and concubines' wives.

literal: Saying dies without a son means the line is cut off and there is no son—not that there is no direct son.
idiomatic: The phrase dies without a son means the line is extinguished and there is no son at all—not that there is no direct heir.

literal: If he had a son, how could one say there was no heir?
idiomatic: If he had a son, how could one say there was no heir?

literal: Though the husband had crippling illness and no son, the wife was still called direct by name.
idiomatic: Even if the husband were crippled and sonless, the wife still bore the name of direct consort.

literal: The name direct being present, yet wishing to set aside her son—how would that accord with ritual!
idiomatic: With the title of direct consort still in place, yet wishing to set aside her son—how would that accord with ritual!

literal: Rites have increase and decrease, generation by generation revising along the way; if one must say the direct heir of the lineage can be changed, then the severest mourning for becoming heir ought also to be altered accordingly.
idiomatic: Rites wax and wane, revised from age to age; if one insists the lineage's direct heir can be changed at will, then the severest mourning for becoming heir ought to change accordingly as well.

literal: In the seventh year, summer, he died, aged fifty-six.
idiomatic: In the seventh year he died in summer, aged fifty-six.

literal: Rou had not long been in the historiography bureau when he met the completion of the enterprise; his intent harbored partisan bias.
idiomatic: Rou had not long served in the historiography bureau when the great compilation was finished; his intent harbored partisan bias.

literal: In the Book of Wei, those with whom he had close kinship inside and outside were all embellished beyond fact; he was deeply ridiculed in the talk of the age.
idiomatic: In the Book of Wei, kinsmen within and outside his circle were all painted brighter than truth; the age ridiculed him sharply for it.

literal: Feng Wei, styled Weijie, was a man of Anxi in Zhongshan.
idiomatic: Feng Wei, styled Weijie, came from Anxi in Zhongshan.

literal: His height was eight chi; cap and robes were very imposing; those who saw him were solemn and held him in awe.
idiomatic: He stood eight chi tall; cap and robes cut an imposing figure, and those who met him felt a solemn awe.

literal: In youth he followed Li Baoding in study; Li valued his quick wit and constantly set him special questions to test him; he understood many things and was especially clear in the Ritual tradition.
idiomatic: In youth he studied under Li Baoding. Li prized his quick wit and constantly set him special tests; he answered most of them, and was especially clear in the Ritual tradition.

literal: Later he returned to his home district, shut his door and did not go out for nearly thirty years, not asking after livelihood, not receiving guests, concentrating his thought alone—there was nothing he did not master.
idiomatic: Later he returned home, shut his door, and for nearly thirty years did not go out—caring nothing for livelihood, receiving no guests, bending all his thought to learning until nothing lay beyond him.

literal: The Prince of Zhao commandery went out to garrison Dingzhou and received him with ritual; orders in writing came three times, and the magistrate came in person to his gate—yet he still pleaded illness and would not rise.
idiomatic: When the Prince of Zhao commandery went out to garrison Dingzhou he received Wei with full ritual courtesy; written summons came three times and the magistrate came to his gate in person—yet Wei still pleaded illness and would not rise.

literal: The prince was about to drive in person to invite him; aides before and behind galloped in relays to report; the magistrate again himself set his cap and shoes in order for him; he had no choice but to go out.
idiomatic: The prince was about to drive out himself to invite him; aides galloped back and forth with reports; the magistrate again arranged cap and shoes for him at the door; at last he had no choice but to go out.

literal: The prince came down from the hall affairs to welcome him, stopped his prostrations, shared the steps going up, lodged him in the guest hostel, and showed him great ritual esteem.
idiomatic: The prince came down from the hall to welcome him, stopped his prostrations, shared the steps as they went up, lodged him in the guest quarters, and honored him with great ceremony.

literal: The prince was about to recommend him as a flourishing talent; he firmly declined and would not accept.
idiomatic: The prince meant to recommend him as a flourishing talent; he firmly declined.

literal: After more than a year he asked to return.
idiomatic: After more than a year he asked to return home.

literal: The prince knew he did not wish to be constrained; he sent him off with ritual and gave rich gifts; he accepted nothing except the seasonal garments of the time.
idiomatic: The prince knew he would not be bound; he sent him off with ritual and rich gifts. Wei accepted nothing but the seasonal garments offered at parting.

literal: On returning he still would not mix in human affairs; the commandery administrator and magistrate each came in person to his gate.
idiomatic: Once home he still would not mix in worldly affairs; commandery administrators and magistrates came in person to his gate.

literal: At the seasons they sometimes set out sheep and wine; he also declined and would not accept.
idiomatic: At the seasons they sometimes sent sheep and wine; he declined those as well.

literal: From disciples, dried meat for the teacher—he did not accept a single strand.
idiomatic: From disciples, the dried meat of tuition—not a single strand would he take.

literal: He plowed for food and raised silkworms for clothing, bamboo basket for rice and gourd dipper for drink, not changing his joy, and in the end died at full years.
idiomatic: He plowed for food and raised silkworms for clothing, ate from a bamboo basket and drank from a gourd dipper, and did not change his joy; in the end he died at full years.

literal: Zhang Mainu was a man of Pingyuan.
idiomatic: Zhang Mainu came from Pingyuan.

literal: His mastery of the classics was comprehensive and broad; his disciples numbered more than a thousand.
idiomatic: His command of the classics was comprehensive; his disciples numbered more than a thousand.

literal: The Confucians all pushed him forward in esteem; his fame and voice were very great.
idiomatic: The Confucians all pushed him forward in esteem, and his fame was very great.

literal: He passed through erudite of the Imperial University and assistant teacher of the National University, and died in the Tianbao era.
idiomatic: He served as erudite of the Imperial University and assistant teacher of the National University, and died in the Tianbao era.

literal: Liu Guisi was a man of Bohai.
idiomatic: Liu Guisi came from Bohai.

literal: His exposition of the Odes was very refined.
idiomatic: His exposition of the Odes was very refined.

literal: In youth he served Liu Jinghe of the same commandery; Jinghe served Cheng Guize of the same commandery—thus in their home district many became students of the Odes.
idiomatic: In youth he studied under Liu Jinghe of the same commandery; Jinghe had studied under Cheng Guize of the same commandery—thus in their home district many became students of the Odes.

literal: Guisi in the Tiantong era served as erudite of the National University.
idiomatic: In the Tiantong era Guisi served as erudite of the National University.

literal: Bao Jixiang was a man of Bohai.
idiomatic: Bao Jixiang came from Bohai.

literal: He was very clear in the Rites; hearing him separate text and parse clauses, one naturally grasped the general meaning.
idiomatic: He was very clear in the Rites; hearing him separate text and parse clauses, one naturally grasped the general meaning.

literal: He was also versed in the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals; in youth he was constantly chief lecturer for Li Baoding, and later also had his own following; the Confucians praised him.
idiomatic: He was also versed in the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals. In youth he had long served as chief lecturer for Li Baoding; later he gathered his own following, and the Confucians praised him.

literal: In the Tiantong era he died as erudite of the Imperial University.
idiomatic: In the Tiantong era he died while serving as erudite of the Imperial University.

literal: His younger cousin Changxuan was also versed in the Ritual tradition.
idiomatic: His younger cousin Changxuan was also versed in the Ritual tradition.

literal: At the end of Wuping he was staff aide to Chancellor Prince of Rencheng Tao, and constantly taught in the capital the sons of noble houses.
idiomatic: At the end of Wuping he was staff aide to Chancellor Prince of Rencheng Tao and constantly taught in the capital the sons of noble houses.

literal: After Qi perished he returned to his home district to lecture on the classics and died at home.
idiomatic: After Qi fell he returned home to lecture on the classics and died there.

literal: Xing Zhi, styled Shijun, was a man of Mo in Hejian; from youth he loved learning, immersed himself in the canonical tomes, and traveled in study between Yan and Zhao, mastering the two Rites and the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.
idiomatic: Xing Zhi, styled Shijun, came from Mo in Hejian. From youth he loved learning, immersed himself in the canonical tomes, and traveled between Yan and Zhao until he mastered the two Rites and the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals.

literal: At the start of Tianbao the commandery recommended him as filial and incorrupt; he was appointed erudite of the Four Gates, promoted to assistant teacher of the National University, and entered the palace to instruct the heir apparent in the classics.
idiomatic: At the start of Tianbao the commandery recommended him as filial and incorrupt; he was appointed erudite of the Four Gates, promoted to assistant teacher of the National University, and entered the palace to instruct the heir apparent in the classics.

literal: Zhi was square, upright, pure, and thick, with the bearing of a Confucian.
idiomatic: Zhi was square, upright, pure, and steadfast, with the bearing of a true Confucian.

literal: The kitchen steward presented the heir apparent's food; there was a dish called xiehao; Zhi ordered it removed and said: This dish has an inauspicious name; it is not what Your Highness should eat.
idiomatic: When the kitchen steward presented the heir apparent's meal, one dish was a herb called xiehao. Zhi ordered it removed and said, "This plant bears an inauspicious name—it is not food fit for Your Highness."

literal: Emperor Xianzu heard and praised this, bestowing quilts and silks, and appointing him erudite of the National University.
idiomatic: Emperor Xianzu heard of it and praised him, bestowing quilts and silks and appointing him erudite of the National University.

literal: At the start of Huangjian he was made administrator of Qinghe; his administration had benevolent policies and officials and people loved him.
idiomatic: At the start of Huangjian he was made administrator of Qinghe; his rule was benevolent, and officials and people loved him.

literal: Because of age he resigned on grounds of illness and returned home, and died at home.
idiomatic: When age weighed on him he resigned on grounds of illness, returned home, and died there.

literal: Liu Zhou, styled Kongzhao, was a man of Fucheng in Bohai.
idiomatic: Liu Zhou, styled Kongzhao, came from Fucheng in Bohai.

literal: Orphaned young and poor, he loved learning, carried a book box and followed teachers, bending his breast without weariness.
idiomatic: Orphaned young and poor, he loved learning, carried his book box from teacher to teacher, and bent to his studies without weariness.

literal: With the Confucian Li Baoding he was of the same home district and very close in affection; he received from him the three Rites.
idiomatic: With the Confucian Li Baoding he shared a home district and deep affection; from Li he received the three Rites.

literal: He also went to Ma Jingde to study the Fu clan Spring and Autumn Annals; both mastered the great meaning.
idiomatic: He also studied the Fu clan Spring and Autumn Annals under Ma Jingde; both mastered the great meaning.

literal: He regretted that in his home district there were few canonical tomes and, staff in hand, entered the capital.
idiomatic: He regretted that his home district held few canonical tomes and, staff in hand, made for the capital.

literal: Knowing that Vice Director of the Imperial Storehouse Song Shiliang's household had many books, he went to him.
idiomatic: Learning that Vice Director of the Imperial Storehouse Song Shiliang's household held many books, he went to him.

literal: Shiliang took him in.
idiomatic: Shiliang took him in.

literal: He read at will day and night without rest.
idiomatic: He read at will, day and night without rest.

literal: At the start of Heqingchu he returned to Jizhou; recommended as a seasonal talent he entered the capital; in the examination composition he did not place.
idiomatic: At the start of Heqingchu he returned to Jizhou; recommended as a seasonal talent he entered the capital, but failed the examination composition.

literal: He then resented not having studied composition, and only then began to weave literary ornament—his language was very archaic and clumsy.
idiomatic: He then resented not having studied composition and only then began to weave literary ornament—his language was very archaic and clumsy.

literal: He composed one fu taking Six Harmonies as its title, calling it peerless, and chanted it without cease.
idiomatic: He composed a fu titled Six Harmonies, called it peerless, and chanted it without cease.

literal: He sighed and said: The Confucian toils yet achieves little—here it is seen.
idiomatic: He sighed and said, "The Confucian toils yet achieves little—here it is seen."

literal: I read Confucian books more than twenty years yet failed the examination composition; I began to study writing and at once could do this.
idiomatic: "I read Confucian books for more than twenty years yet failed the examination; I began to study writing and at once could do this."

literal: He once presented this fu to Wei Shou; Shou told others: The fu is named Six Harmonies—its folly is already great; when I saw the fu, it was more foolish than the name.
idiomatic: He once presented this fu to Wei Shou. Shou told others, "The fu is named Six Harmonies—its folly is already great; when I saw the fu, it was more foolish than the name."

literal: Zhou also composed three pieces of the Biography of Great Talent Unrewarded.
idiomatic: Zhou also composed three pieces of the Biography of Great Talent Unrewarded.

literal: In the Huangjian and Daning reigns he again repeatedly submitted memorials; his words were also blunt and direct, mostly not what the age required, and in the end he was never accepted and employed.
idiomatic: In the Huangjian and Daning reigns he again and again submitted memorials—blunt and direct, mostly unwelcome to the age—and in the end was never employed.

literal: He considered himself broadly learned and a rare talent, spoke fondly in grand terms, and often said: Let a few dozen volumes of mine circulate in later ages—it is no harder than Duke Jing of Qi's thousand four-horse teams.
idiomatic: He considered himself broadly learned and a rare talent, spoke in fond grand terms, and often said, "Let a few dozen volumes of mine circulate in later ages—it is no harder than Duke Jing of Qi's thousand four-horse teams."

literal: Yet his bearing was easy and slow, his movements not of the proper kind—because of this in the end he had no advancement in office.
idiomatic: Yet his bearing was easy and slow and his movements ill-suited to propriety—because of this he never advanced in office.

literal: In the Tiantong era he died at home, aged fifty-two.
idiomatic: In the Tiantong era he died at home, aged fifty-two.

literal: Ma Jingde was a man of Hejian.
idiomatic: Ma Jingde came from Hejian.

literal: In youth he loved Confucian studies, carried a book box and followed the great Confucian Xu Zunming in studying the Odes and Rites, grasping the great meaning but unable to refine it.
idiomatic: In youth he loved Confucian studies, carried his book box, and followed the great Confucian Xu Zunming in the Odes and Rites—grasping the great meaning but unable to refine it.

literal: He then turned his mind to the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, pondering and seeking deeply day and night without weariness; his explication of meaning was praised by the Confucians.
idiomatic: He then turned his mind to the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals, pondering it day and night without weariness; his explication of meaning won praise from the Confucians.
